summaries.example: Imagine a town paying for a lighthouse. Once its light shines, many boats can use it, and it is hard to stop one boat from benefiting. One boat’s use usually does not leave less light for another.
summaries.summary: A public good is usually a good that people can enjoy together without reducing one another’s enjoyment and that is difficult to keep anyone from using. National defence, clean air, and some forms of public safety are examples. This definition is about how a good works, not simply about whether the government provides it. Food and clothing are private goods because one person’s use leaves less for others and owners can usually keep non-payers out. Other goods, such as fish stocks or cinema seats, have one public-good feature but not the other. The boundaries can change with technology, laws, social rules, and crowding. Public goods can create benefits for people who did not help produce them. That makes free riding tempting and can lead to too little being provided. Governments may help, but private groups, businesses, donations, fairness rules, and social habits can also help. The entry also asks whether government payment is always fair or wise, since public decisions involve knowledge, rights, equality, and competing values.
key_ideas: A public good is usually defined by two features: people can share its benefits without using them up, and it is difficult to keep people from benefiting.
Public goods are not necessarily goods supplied by the government. A private group or business can sometimes provide them.
Goods do not fit into fixed boxes forever. Technology, laws, customs, and the situation can change whether something is rivalrous or excludable.
Public goods can be local, national, or global. A playground may help nearby children, while climate protection can help people around the world.
Because everyone may benefit, people may wait for others to pay. This is called the free-rider problem. Still, experiments and real-life cases show that people often contribute voluntarily.
summaries.why_it_matters: Public goods help societies work: roads and safety support daily life, education can support democracy, and clean environments benefit many people. Understanding them helps us ask who should provide shared benefits, how people can cooperate, and whether a policy helps everyone fairly.

important_terms.definition: Something that people can use or benefit from, such as food, a road, or protection.
A good is rivalrous when one person’s use leaves less available for someone else. One person eating a sandwich prevents another from eating that same sandwich.
A good is excludable when it is possible to stop people from using it. A locked house is excludable.
A good that is both non-rivalrous and non-excludable. National defence is a common example.
Getting the benefit without helping pay or work for it. This can make people hope that others will contribute instead.

questions_to_think_about: Can you think of something many people use that is hard to keep people away from?
Is a public park always a public good, or could rules and crowded spaces change its features?
Why might someone contribute even when they could benefit without contributing?
Should a town pay for a good if some people benefit more than others?

summaries.example: Suppose residents fund a radio broadcast. Once it exists, a non-contributor may still hear it, and one listener’s hearing normally does not prevent another’s. The situation creates a benefit for outsiders and an incentive to free ride, even when the residents together value the broadcast more than it costs to produce.
summaries.summary: The entry examines public goods through economics and political philosophy. In the standard account, a public good combines non-rivalry—one person’s benefit does not reduce another’s ability to benefit—with non-excludability—people cannot readily be prevented from benefiting. National defence is paradigmatic, while food and housing are standard private goods. Common-pool resources and club goods occupy the other two positions in the rivalry/exclusion scheme. These categories are porous: congestion, enforcement, property rights, technology, norms, and changing tastes affect classification. The same good may therefore be public in one setting and less public in another. Public goods typically create positive externalities, although positive spillovers alone do not establish public-good status. Their provision produces a strategic problem. Each person may prefer a collectively funded good but also prefer that others bear its cost. A simple model predicts underprovision, while experiments and field evidence show contributions, cooperation, social norms, altruism, and learning. The entry considers government funding, private provision through linked private benefits, and mechanisms intended to reveal preferences. It then questions whether efficiency arguments settle the ethical issue. Preference satisfaction may be unstable or uninformed; interpersonal comparisons are difficult; compensation may not occur; and rights, equality, justice, and democratic values may conflict with market provision or coercive taxation. Kallhoff’s alternative emphasizes basic availability and open access, while related arguments stress public goods’ role in democratic connection and shared citizenship.
key_ideas: The standard economic definition treats public goods as both non-rivalrous and non-excludable. This distinguishes them from private goods, common-pool resources, and club goods.
The classification is contextual rather than perfectly fixed. Congestion, legal rights, enforcement costs, technology, tastes, and social norms can alter a good’s degree of rivalry or excludability.
Public goods can be local, national, global, or partial. A parade may be public for people watching from nearby buildings but more private for people who need paid seats.
Public goods generate positive externalities, but not every positive externality is a public good. A benefit can spill over to others without being non-rivalrous or non-excludable.

The standard public-goods model resembles a Prisoner’s Dilemma: everyone may prefer joint contribution, yet each individual has an incentive to let others pay. Experiments, however, find substantial voluntary contribution and mixed motives.

Government provision is not automatically justified. Arguments about efficient supply must also confront hidden preferences, paternalism, rights, unequal effects, fairness, and the information provided by markets.
summaries.why_it_matters: Public goods connect abstract economic categories to decisions about education, security, infrastructure, public health, science, and the environment. The topic matters because deciding how to provide shared benefits involves not only incentives and efficiency but also information, coercion, equality, democratic participation, and the norms appropriate to different kinds of goods.

important_terms.definition: A good is non-rivalrous when one person’s consumption does not diminish other people’s ability to consume it.
A good is non-excludable when preventing people from benefiting from it is impossible or sufficiently difficult, given technology, law, and social arrangements.
A good that is rivalrous but non-excludable, such as fish stocks. Use by some can leave less for others, yet exclusion may be difficult.
A good that is non-rivalrous but excludable, such as some cinema or membership services. Access can be restricted even when use is largely shared.
An effect of a transaction on people who are not parties to it. Pollution is a negative externality; pollination benefiting a neighboring orchard is a positive one.
The incentive to receive a public good’s benefits while avoiding a contribution to its cost.
An outcome in which at least one person is better off and no one is worse off than in another outcome.
A proposed alternative to the usual definition, emphasizing equal basic availability of benefits and open access rather than the standard labels alone.

questions_to_think_about: If a road has tolls and becomes congested, how might its classification change?
Does the existence of a positive externality show that something is a public good? Why or why not?
Why can voluntary contributions exceed the prediction of a purely self-interested model, yet still fall below the socially efficient level?
Would a policy that makes some people better off and others worse off count as a Pareto improvement?
Should public goods be distributed according to preferences, needs, equality, or some other principle?

summaries.example: A group of students wants to keep a shared school garden clean. Everyone enjoys the garden, including students who do not help. Each student may hope that others will do the work, but the garden stays nicer when enough people cooperate. A rule, a shared sense of fairness, or seeing others help may encourage contributions.
summaries.summary: The entry explains why economists and philosophers care about public goods. The usual definition combines two ideas: non-rivalry, meaning that one person’s use does not reduce another person’s possible use, and non-excludability, meaning that it is difficult to stop people from benefiting. National defence, clean air, and some kinds of public safety fit this pattern. Private goods such as food are rivalrous and excludable. Common-pool resources, such as fish stocks, are rivalrous but difficult to restrict, while club goods can be shared by members but kept from non-members. These categories are not permanent. Crowding, laws, property rights, enforcement, technology, and social expectations can change how a good works. Public goods often create positive externalities: people outside the original transaction receive benefits. This can lead to the free-rider problem. In a simple model, everyone may prefer that a shared good exist, but each person has a reason to let others pay. Economists study government solutions, private arrangements, and special systems for learning how much people value a good. Evidence from experiments and real settings suggests that people are not motivated only by narrow self-interest. Fairness, generosity, communication, and social rules can support cooperation. The philosophical debate continues because efficient production does not by itself answer questions about rights, equality, democratic values, or whether government should compel payment.
key_ideas: Whether something is a public good depends on rivalry and exclusion, not simply on whether the government supplies it.
The four broad categories are private goods, public goods, common-pool resources, and club goods. Real examples can sit near the boundaries.
Technology and rules matter. Radio was once harder to restrict, while digital systems can make exclusion easier.
A public good can help people who did not pay for it, creating a positive externality. But a positive externality by itself does not prove that a good is public.

The free-rider problem explains why people may support a shared project but choose not to contribute. Experiments show that people often contribute anyway, though contributions can decline over repeated rounds.
Some philosophers argue that government provision may protect fairness or democratic participation. Others point to limits involving taxes, rights, knowledge, and unequal benefits.
summaries.why_it_matters: Public goods are part of everyday collective life. Thinking about them helps explain why communities create rules, why cooperation can be difficult, and why debates about taxes and shared services cannot be settled by cost alone. It also shows why one label may not fit a good in every place or period.

important_terms.definition: A good that one person can use without leaving less for others to use.
A good that is difficult to keep people from using or enjoying.
A good that is both non-rivalrous and non-excludable.
A spillover effect of an activity on people who were not part of the original exchange.
Benefiting from a shared good while avoiding a fair share of its cost.
A good that can be used by some but becomes less available through use, while excluding users is difficult.
A shared service that can be limited to members of a group, such as some club services.

questions_to_think_about: What makes the school garden resemble a public good, and what might make it different?
Can a good become excludable because of a new technology?
Why might people cooperate even when free riding seems easier?
Is government funding justified whenever a good benefits many people?
How could a shared good help democracy beyond its direct practical benefit?
